```{r helpers, echo=FALSE}
draw_workflow <- function(highlight = NULL, cex = 0.9) {
  boxes <- c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES", "MODELS", "FIT", "COMPARE")
  subs <- c("what do we\nneed to know?", "candidate\nexplanations",
            "data-generating\n(process + noise)", "confront each\nwith data",
            "fit, prediction,\nrelevance")
  x <- seq(1, 9, by = 2)
  y <- 2
  w <- 0.8
  h <- 0.55
  shade <- function(lab) if (!is.null(highlight) && lab %in% highlight) "lightskyblue1" else "white"
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-0.2, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(boxes)) {
    rect(x[i] - w, y - h, x[i] + w, y + h, col = shade(boxes[i]), lwd = 1.5)
    text(x[i], y + 0.18, boxes[i], font = 2, cex = cex)
    text(x[i], y - 0.22, subs[i], cex = cex * 0.75)
  }
  arrows(x[-5] + w, y, x[-1] - w, y, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  rect(6 - 0.7, 3.2 - 0.35, 6 + 0.7, 3.2 + 0.35, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 3.28, "DATA", font = 2, cex = cex)
  text(6, 3.0, "study design", cex = cex * 0.75)
  arrows(x[3], y + h, 6 - 0.7, 3.2, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(6 + 0.7, 3.2, x[4], y + h, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  segments(x[5], y - h, x[5], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(x[5], 0.4, x[1], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  arrows(x[c(1, 2)], 0.4, x[c(1, 2)], y - h, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 0.15, "REVISE the problem and theories; drop or down-weight poor models",
       cex = cex * 0.85, font = 3)
}

# map helpers: a grid variable as an image, plots as colored points, fire perimeters as lines
pal_seq <- hcl.colors(64, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE)
pal_div <- hcl.colors(65, "Blue-Red 3")
val_col <- function(v, zlim, pal) pal[pmax(1, pmin(length(pal), 1 + floor((v - zlim[1]) / diff(zlim) * length(pal))))]
map_base <- function(main = "", ...) {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 40), ylim = c(0, 30), asp = 1, xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
       xlab = "Easting (km)", ylab = "Northing (km)", main = main, cex.main = 0.95, ...)
}
map_image <- function(v, zlim, pal, main = "") {
  map_base(main)
  image(ux, uy, matrix(pmax(zlim[1], pmin(zlim[2], v)), length(ux)), zlim = zlim, col = pal, add = TRUE)
  box()
}
map_fires <- function(...) contour(ux, uy, matrix(grid$burned, length(ux)), levels = 0.5,
                                   drawlabels = FALSE, add = TRUE, ...)
map_key <- function(zlim, pal, title, digits = 1) {
  at <- seq(zlim[1], zlim[2], length.out = 5)
  legend("topright", legend = formatC(at, format = "f", digits = digits), pch = 22, pt.cex = 1.6,
         pt.bg = val_col(at, zlim, pal), col = "grey30", bg = "white", cex = 0.72, title = title)
}
```

# Spatial regression {#spatial}

Waldo Tobler's "first law of geography" reads: "Everything is related
to everything else, but near things are more related than distant
things."^[Tobler stated it in passing in a 1970 paper simulating urban
growth around Detroit (*Economic Geography* 46: 234-240). Geographers
have argued since about whether it deserves the word "law" (see the 2004
forum in *Annals of the Association of American Geographers*, vol. 94).
Treat it as an empirical regularity that usually holds, not a
guarantee; the [variogram](#variogram) is one way to check it in a
given data set.] 

In a regression model, we can translate Tobler's law to mean that 
observations close together in space tend
to be alike in ways even our covariates can't fully explain, so their residuals
are correlated! One consequence of this is that a model that ignores 
spatially correlated residuals is often overconfident (confidence bounds too narrow).

One way to measure that correlation is
with a variogram (or semivariogram). One way to model it is with a 
Gaussian process (GP) over the 2D spatial domain (the map coordinates).

Here, we fit the same model three ways: by hand, and with `glmmTMB` and
`sdmTMB` (a Bayesian fit with `R-INLA` is a bonus). Finally, we'll walk through the GAM alternative (a smooth across the
lat/long or projected coordinates), and some advice on choosing among the available methods.

## 1. Nearby plots are alike {#problem}

Cheatgrass (*Bromus tectorum*) is an annual grass that has taken over
sagebrush across large parts of the Great Basin, and it promotes a rapid fire cycle 
that tends to favor ... well, more cheatgrass. 

A Bureau of Land Management (BLM) district office surveys 200 plots
across a 40 by 30 km area of public rangeland and measures peak-season
cheatgrass biomass in each (grams per square meter). Three fires have
burned in the area since 2000. The district has two questions:

1. **How much does a past fire raise cheatgrass biomass?**
2. **Where, including places nobody sampled, is biomass high enough to
   need treatment?**

The first question is about a regression coefficient, while the second is about 
spatial projection (a predictive map!). 

This page addresses the first question, and then the 
[worked analysis](#demo) tries to answer both questions!

```{r read-data}
cg <- read.csv("data/CheatgrassSurvey.csv")
grid <- read.csv("data/CheatgrassGrid.csv")
cg$elev_km <- (cg$elev_m - 1800) / 1000         # km above 1800 m
grid$elev_km <- (grid$elev_m - 1800) / 1000
head(cg)
```

The response variable is log cheatgrass biomass. As for predictors, we
have (1) coordinates in kilometers (easting and northing), (2)
elevation, and (3) whether the plot is inside or outside the perimeter
of a recent fire. A roadless block in the south has no plots. These
data are simulated, so the true parameter values are known.^[The
script that generated the data is
[sim_Week14_cheatgrass.R](rcode/sim_Week14_cheatgrass.R).]

```{r data-map, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=5.2}
ux <- sort(unique(grid$x_km))
uy <- sort(unique(grid$y_km))
zl_y <- c(1, 5.5)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
map_base("Cheatgrass survey: 200 plots")
contour(ux, uy, matrix(grid$elev_m, length(ux)), levels = seq(1400, 2400, 100), col = "grey70", add = TRUE,
        labcex = 0.6)
map_fires(lwd = 2, lty = 2)
points(cg$x_km, cg$y_km, pch = ifelse(cg$burned == 1, 24, 21), bg = val_col(cg$log_biomass, zl_y, pal_seq),
       cex = 1.25)
rect(13, 1, 22, 10, border = "grey40", lty = 3)
text(17.5, 5.5, "roadless\n(no plots)", cex = 0.75, col = "grey30")
map_key(zl_y, pal_seq, "log biomass")
legend("bottomright", c("burned plot", "unburned plot", "fire perimeter", "elevation (m)"), pch = c(24, 21, NA, NA),
       lty = c(NA, NA, 2, 1), lwd = c(NA, NA, 2, 1), col = c("black", "black", "black", "grey70"), bg = "white", cex = 0.72)
```

Let's start with an ordinary linear regression of log biomass on fire and elevation:

```{r lm-fit}
fit_lm <- lm(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km, data = cg)
round(summary(fit_lm)$coefficients, 3)
```

```{r lm-numbers, echo=FALSE}
lm_tab <- summary(fit_lm)$coefficients
```

The regression says burned plots have `r f2(lm_tab["burned", 1])` more
log biomass (SE `r f2(lm_tab["burned", 2])`), which is
`r f1(exp(lm_tab["burned", 1]))` times the biomass of unburned plots at
the same elevation. Before believing the standard error, map the
residuals:

```{r lm-resid-map, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.9}
cg$resid_lm <- resid(fit_lm)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
map_base("Residuals from the ordinary regression")
map_fires(lty = 2, col = "grey40")
points(cg$x_km, cg$y_km, pch = 21, cex = 0.5 + 1.6 * abs(cg$resid_lm),
       bg = ifelse(cg$resid_lm > 0, "#c0392b", "#2a78d6"))
legend("topright", c("above the fitted value", "below the fitted value"), pch = 21,
       pt.bg = c("#c0392b", "#2a78d6"), bg = "white", cex = 0.75, title = "symbol size = |residual|")
```

> **Question:** `lm()` assumes the residuals are independent draws from
> one Normal distribution. What on this map says otherwise? If an
> important covariate were missing from the model, what would its map
> look like?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* same-sign residuals cluster (blue patches in the southwest and
the southeast corner; red along the northern edge and around easting 27,
northing 6). A missing covariate would look like this map: smooth patches.
```

Positive residuals sit next to positive ones, and negative next to
negative: Tobler's law still holds after fire and elevation are in the
model. Some spatially correlated variable we didn't measure (soil texture, grazing history,
where seed arrived first) seems to be influencing our response. The `r sum(cg$burned)` burned plots sit in
three fires, so they share it too: they are not `r sum(cg$burned)`
independent looks at what fire does. This is conceptually the same idea as the "two-cores-from-one-tree"
problem from [Week 11's random intercept example](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#random-intercept),
without the tidy groups.

Because the data are simulated, we can see how this can affect our interpretation. 

The code below draws 2000 new surveys from the true model (same plots, same
fires, a new landscape of unmeasured variation each time) and refits
the regression to each.

```{r design-and-distances}
library(mvtnorm)
X <- model.matrix(~ burned + elev_km, data = cg)
D <- as.matrix(dist(cg[, c("x_km", "y_km")]))            # distances between plots (km)
```

```{r lm-coverage, cache=TRUE}
V_true <- 0.7^2 * exp(-D / 6) + 0.3^2 * diag(nrow(cg))   # the covariance the data came from
set.seed(746)
Y <- rmvnorm(2000, X %*% c(3, 0.5, -2), V_true)          # truth: fire effect 0.5
sims <- t(apply(Y, 1, function(y) summary(lm(y ~ X - 1))$coefficients[2, 1:2]))
c(sd_of_estimates = sd(sims[, 1]), mean_reported_se = mean(sims[, 2]),
  coverage_95 = mean(abs(sims[, 1] - 0.5) < qt(0.975, 197) * sims[, 2]))
```

The fire estimates vary from survey to survey with an SD of
`r f2(sd(sims[, 1]))`, but `lm()` reports a standard error near
`r f2(mean(sims[, 2]))`, so its 95% intervals contain the true effect
only `r round(100 * mean(abs(sims[, 1] - 0.5) < qt(0.975, 197) * sims[, 2]))`%
of the time.^[The exact answer needs no simulation. If the errors have
covariance $V$, the least-squares estimate
$\hat\beta = (X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty$ has covariance
$(X^TX)^{-1}X^T V X (X^TX)^{-1}$, which reduces to the usual
$\sigma^2 (X^TX)^{-1}$ only when $V = \sigma^2 I$. With the true $V$
here the SE of the fire coefficient is
`r f2(sqrt((solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X) %*% V_true %*% X %*% solve(t(X) %*% X))[2, 2]))`.]
The survey in hand happens to be one where the estimate landed well
above the truth of 0.5.

## 2. The variogram {#variogram}

What is the scale of spatial correlation in this system? 

Take every pair of plots, and
compare the difference in their residuals with the distance between
them. The **semivariance**^[The "semi" is the factor of ½, which puts
the curve on the variance scale. If two residuals each have variance
$\sigma^2$ and covariance $C(d)$, then
$E[(e_i - e_j)^2] = 2\sigma^2 - 2C(d)$, so $\gamma(d) = \sigma^2 - C(d)$:
the variogram is the covariance function turned upside down, and it
levels off at the variance itself (the sill) once $C(d)$ reaches zero.
There are two reasons to work with differences rather than estimate
$C(d)$ directly. A constant mean cancels in $e_i - e_j$, so it needn't
be estimated first (with correlated data an estimated mean is
imprecise, and it biases covariance estimates low). And the variogram
stays defined for processes whose variance keeps growing as the area
grows, such as a random walk across the landscape, as long as
differences over a fixed distance are well behaved. Some sources call
$2\gamma(d)$ the variogram and $\gamma(d)$ the semivariogram; `gstat`
and this page call the plot of $\gamma$ the variogram.] at distance $d$ is half the average squared
difference between residuals of plots about $d$ apart:

$$\hat\gamma(d) = \frac{1}{2\,N(d)} \sum_{\text{pairs } i,j \text{ about } d \text{ apart}} (e_i - e_j)^2$$

If nearby plots are alike, $\hat\gamma$ is small at short distances and
rises as the plots get farther apart. A plot of $\hat\gamma$ against
distance is a **variogram**.

```{r variogram}
library(gstat)
library(sp)
cg_sp <- cg
coordinates(cg_sp) <- ~ x_km + y_km
vg_lm <- variogram(resid_lm ~ 1, cg_sp, cutoff = 20, width = 2)     # 2-km distance bins
vg_lm[, c("np", "dist", "gamma")]
```

```{r variogram-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(vg_lm$dist, vg_lm$gamma, pch = 16, xlim = c(0, 20), ylim = c(0, 0.7), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
     xlab = "Distance between plots (km)", ylab = "Semivariance of residuals")
abline(h = var(cg$resid_lm), lty = 2, col = "grey50")
text(19.5, var(cg$resid_lm) + 0.03, "variance of all residuals", adj = 1, cex = 0.8, col = "grey30")
```

Three features of a variogram have names:

- the **nugget**, where the curve meets the vertical axis: the variance
  between plots that are practically on top of each other (measurement
  error and very fine-scale variation);
- the **sill**, where it levels off: the total variance, reached by
  plots too far apart to share anything;
- the **range**, the distance at which it gets there.

Here plots 1 km apart differ much less
(semivariance `r f2(vg_lm$gamma[1])`) than plots 10 km apart
(`r f2(vg_lm$gamma[vg_lm$dist > 9][1])`), and the curve flattens
somewhere around 8 to 12 km.^[A one-number summary of the same thing is
Moran's $I$, a correlation between each residual and a
distance-weighted average of its neighbors (`ape::Moran.I()`). It makes
a quick test for "is there any spatial pattern?", but it doesn't say
how far the pattern reaches, and a model needs to know.]

The covariance function measures how similar two residuals are at
distance $d$; the variogram measures how different they are. To
connect the two, split each residual into two pieces. One varies
smoothly across the landscape: it has variance $\sigma_s^2$, and its
values at two plots $d$ apart have correlation $\rho(d)$. The other is
plot-level noise, independent from plot to plot, with variance
$\sigma_e^2$. Then

$$\gamma(d) = \sigma_e^2 + \sigma_s^2\,\bigl(1 - \rho(d)\bigr)$$

so the nugget is $\sigma_e^2$, the sill is $\sigma_s^2 + \sigma_e^2$,
and the shape of the rise is the correlation function turned upside
down. The widget simulates a landscape from this model, samples 150
plots, and draws both the model's variogram and the one computed from
the plots.

```{r widget-variogram, echo=FALSE}
widget("variogram.html")
```

> **Question:** Set the nugget SD to 0 and then raise it to 0.8. What
> changes on the map, and what changes in the variogram? Then set it
> back to 0.3 and move the length-scale from 1 to 10 km. At which
> setting would 150 plots give you the most independent information
> about the landscape's mean?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* the nugget adds plot-level noise the map can't show and lifts
the whole variogram curve. Most independent information at a
length-scale of 1 km: plots more than a few km apart are nearly
independent, so 150 plots are close to 150 looks. At 10 km the
landscape has only a handful of independent patches.
```

## 3. A Gaussian process over the map {#gp-space}

Let's model that variogram! This really just adds one term to the
regression:

$$y_i = \mathbf{x}_i^T\boldsymbol\beta + s_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
\mathbf{s} \sim \text{MVN}(\mathbf{0},\ \sigma_s^2 R), \qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_e^2)$$

where $s_i$ is the value at plot $i$ of a **spatial random field**: a
surface of unmeasured variation, with one value at every point on the
map.^[For an interactive introduction to Gaussian processes, see
[A Visual Exploration of Gaussian Processes](https://distill.pub/2019/visual-exploration-gaussian-processes/)
(Görtler, Kehlbeck, and Deussen 2019, *Distill*).] The correlation between its values at two plots depends on the
distance $d_{ij}$ between them. The simplest choice is the exponential
correlation function,

$$R_{ij} = \exp(-d_{ij}/\ell)$$

with **length-scale** $\ell$ in km. Adding the pieces, all 200
observations are one draw from a multivariate Normal:

$$\mathbf{y} \sim \text{MVN}(X\boldsymbol\beta,\ V), \qquad
V = \sigma_s^2 R + \sigma_e^2 I$$

This should look familiar. At its core is the
[structured covariance matrix](Week12_MixedModels.html#mixed-models-r) that has 
allowed us to model non-independence of observations over these last 
few weeks! Recall:

- a [random intercept](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#random-intercept)
  puts $\sigma_a^2$ wherever two observations share a group;
- [AR(1)](Week12_MixedModels.html#ar1) puts $\phi^{|s-t|}$ wherever two
  observations are $|s-t|$ years apart, which is the exponential
  function above with time in place of distance ($\phi = e^{-1/\ell}$);
- the [Gaussian process](Week13_HierarchicalModelsAndGAMs.html#gp) for
  the Bd growth curve used the gap in temperature between two cultures.
  The spatial field $\mathbf{s}$ is a Gaussian process too, with a kernel
  that takes the distance (e.g., in km) between two observations.^[Last week's
  amplitude $\alpha$ is this page's $\sigma_s$. Geostatistics arrived
  at the same model decades before machine learning named it a
  Gaussian process, which is why the vocabulary (nugget, sill, range,
  kriging) is different.]

It is also a [hierarchical model](Week13_HierarchicalModelsAndGAMs.html#what-hierarchical):
the data are conditionally independent given the field, plus a model for the field, with hyperparameters 
(length scale, amplitude) also fitted using the data. 

Just like with mixed models, when we write the likelihood as one single MVN
with $V$ it is called the *marginal* form, because it integrates the field itself
out of the likelihood: the field enters only through the variances and
covariances in $V$.

So the likelihood becomes one `dmvnorm()` call that we can fit using `optim()`.
The parameters are just the three regression coefficients and the
$\sigma_s$, $\ell$, and $\sigma_e$ terms (usually log transformed so `optim()` doesn't
try to explore negative variances!).

```{r by-hand}
y <- cg$log_biomass
nll_spatial <- function(par) {
  beta <- par[1:3]
  sigma_s <- exp(par[4])
  ell <- exp(par[5])
  sigma_e <- exp(par[6])
  V <- sigma_s^2 * exp(-D / ell) + sigma_e^2 * diag(length(y))
  -dmvnorm(y, as.vector(X %*% beta), V, log = TRUE)
}
fit_hand <- optim(c(coef(fit_lm), log(0.5), log(5), log(0.5)), nll_spatial, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)
se_hand <- sqrt(diag(solve(fit_hand$hessian)))
est_hand <- c(fit_hand$par[1:3], exp(fit_hand$par[4:6]))
names(est_hand) <- c("intercept", "burned", "elev_km", "sigma_s", "ell", "sigma_e")
round(est_hand, 3)
round(rbind(lm = c(coef(fit_lm)[2:3], sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_lm)))[2:3]),
            spatial = c(fit_hand$par[2:3], se_hand[2:3])), 3)        # estimates, then SEs
c(logLik_lm = as.numeric(logLik(fit_lm)), logLik_spatial = -fit_hand$value)
```

```{r by-hand-numbers, echo=FALSE}
aic_lm <- AIC(fit_lm)
aic_hand <- 2 * fit_hand$value + 2 * 6
```

Three things changed.

- **The fire effect size is reduced**, from `r f2(coef(fit_lm)[2])` to
  `r f2(fit_hand$par[2])` (truth 0.5). The regression compared burned
  plots with every unburned plot on the map. The spatial model leans more heavily on
  comparisons between burned plots and *nearby* unburned ones, which
  share the same unmeasured conditions.
- **The fire effect is more uncertain.** Its standard error grew from `r f2(lm_tab["burned", 2])` to
  `r f2(se_hand[2])`, because plots inside one fire are no longer
  counted as independent (we now have a lower effective sample size).
- **The elevation SE tripled**, from `r f2(lm_tab["elev_km", 2])` to
  `r f2(se_hand[3])`. Elevation changes slowly across the map, and so does
  the field, and the data can't fully tell them apart. This is what's known in the biz
  as **spatial confounding**.

The spatial model has two more parameters and improves the
log-likelihood by `r f1(-fit_hand$value - as.numeric(logLik(fit_lm)))`
(AIC `r f1(aic_hand)` against `r f1(aic_lm)`). The estimated
length-scale is $\hat\ell =$ `r f1(est_hand["ell"])` km: two plots that
far apart have a field correlation of $e^{-1} = 0.37$, and at
$2\hat\ell =$ `r f1(2 * est_hand["ell"])` km it is down to
$e^{-2} \approx 0.13$. Packages report that second distance, where
correlation has fallen to about 0.13, as the **range**.

```{r variogram-fit-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(vg_lm$dist, vg_lm$gamma, pch = 16, xlim = c(0, 20), ylim = c(0, 0.7), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
     xlab = "Distance between plots (km)", ylab = "Semivariance of residuals")
curve(est_hand["sigma_e"]^2 + est_hand["sigma_s"]^2 * (1 - exp(-x / est_hand["ell"])), add = TRUE, lwd = 2.5,
      col = "#2a78d6")
abline(h = est_hand["sigma_e"]^2, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
text(19.5, est_hand["sigma_e"]^2 + 0.03, "nugget", adj = 1, cex = 0.8, col = "grey30")
legend("bottomright", c("lm residuals", "fitted spatial model"), pch = c(16, NA), lwd = c(NA, 2.5),
       col = c("black", "#2a78d6"), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

The above variogram was computed from `lm()` residuals, and the fitted
curve comes from maximizing the likelihood.^[Older geostatistics fit
the curve to the variogram points by least squares and then predicted
in a second step. Maximum likelihood fits the coefficients and the
covariance parameters together and gives standard errors for all of
them.]

The exponential is one member of the **Matérn** family, a flexible
family of correlation functions that is the usual choice in spatial
statistics. The mesh-based packages below use a Matérn field; the
[bonus section](#bonus-matern) has more details.

## 4. A mesh makes it fast {#mesh}

```{r chol-timing, echo=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(1)
time_chol <- sapply(c(1000, 2000, 4000), function(n) {
  V <- exp(-as.matrix(dist(cbind(runif(n, 0, 40), runif(n, 0, 30)))) / 4) + diag(0.1, n)
  system.time(chol(V))[["elapsed"]]
})
```

Every likelihood evaluation above factors a 200 by 200 matrix, which
takes a few milliseconds.^[To factor $V$ here means a Cholesky
decomposition, $V = LL^T$ with $L$ lower triangular. It gives
everything the multivariate Normal likelihood needs without ever
forming $V^{-1}$: $\log|V| = 2\sum_i \log L_{ii}$, and for the
residual vector $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol\beta$, solving
$L\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{r}$ for $\mathbf{z}$ (one row at a time, from
the top) gives $\mathbf{r}^T V^{-1}\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{z}$.] The work grows with the cube of the number of
plots ([why correlated-data models are hard](Week12_MixedModels.html#harder)):
on the computer that built this page one factorization took
`r f2(time_chol[1])` seconds for 1000 plots, `r f2(time_chol[2])` for
2000, and `r f1(time_chol[3])` for 4000. At that rate 20,000 plots
(a modest camera-trap or eBird data set) would take about
`r round(time_chol[3] * 125 / 60)` minutes per evaluation, and
`optim()` needs hundreds.

The fix used by `sdmTMB` and `R-INLA` goes back to the key idea from last
week's lecture on splines and GAMs: [build the function from basis functions](Week13_HierarchicalModelsAndGAMs.html#basis).
Cover the study area with a **mesh** of triangles. Give the field one
unknown value at each vertex, and let its value anywhere else be a
weighted average of the three vertices of the triangle it falls in:

$$s(\text{location}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k\,\psi_k(\text{location})$$

Each basis function $\psi_k$ is a little tent: 1 at vertex $k$, falling
to 0 at the neighboring vertices. These are the two-dimensional version
of the degree-1 B-splines ("tent basis") in last week's spline widget, and the
vertices are analogous to knots.

```{r mesh}
library(sdmTMB)
mesh <- make_mesh(cg, xy_cols = c("x_km", "y_km"), cutoff = 2)     # no two vertices closer than 2 km
mesh$mesh$n                                                        # number of vertices
```

```{r mesh-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5}
par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(mesh$mesh, main = "", asp = 1)
points(cg$x_km, cg$y_km, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "#c0392b")
```

The mesh extends past the study area so the edge of the mesh doesn't
distort the field near the outermost plots (boundary effects).

Each plot's field value is
a weighted average of at most three vertex values, so the matrix that
maps vertex values to plots is mostly zeros (that is, it is a **sparse matrix**, which can have huge computational advantages!):

```{r mesh-projection}
A <- fmesher::fm_basis(mesh$mesh, loc = as.matrix(cg[, c("x_km", "y_km")]))
dim(A)                                    # 200 plots by K vertices
i <- which(Matrix::rowSums(A != 0) == 3)[1]
A[i, A[i, ] != 0]                         # one plot's three weights
```

```{r mesh-sparsity, echo=FALSE}
Q_demo <- fmesher::fm_matern_precision(mesh$mesh, alpha = 2, rho = 8, sigma = 0.6)
q_per_row <- Matrix::nnzero(Q_demo) / nrow(Q_demo)
```

The second half of the idea is the prior on the vertex values
$\mathbf{w}$. Lindgren, Rue, and Lindström (2011) showed how to choose
a multivariate Normal for $\mathbf{w}$ so that the tent-function
surface behaves like a Gaussian process with Matérn covariance, and so
that the **precision matrix** $Q = \Sigma^{-1}$ of $\mathbf{w}$ is
sparse: each vertex is tied directly only to vertices a step or two
away. For this mesh $Q$ averages `r f1(q_per_row)` nonzero entries per
row, out of `r mesh$mesh$n`. Sparse matrices factor in far less time
than dense ones! In this approach, the cost grows with the number of vertices,
not the number of plots.^[This is called the SPDE approach, because the
link between the Matérn covariance and a sparse $Q$ comes from a
stochastic partial differential equation whose solutions are Matérn
fields (Lindgren et al. 2011, *J. R. Stat. Soc. B* 73: 423-498). You
can use it without the equation. An AR(1) series has the same property
in one dimension: its covariance matrix $\phi^{|s-t|}$ is full, but its
precision matrix is tridiagonal, since each year is tied directly only
to the years before and after.]

Compare the "smooth functions" we constructed from basis functions last week.
A penalized spline is a linear model (basis functions times weights), with a
penalty on the weights to limit wiggliness. A Gaussian process does the
same job with a covariance function (a kernel) in place of basis
functions. The mesh version of a random field approximates a Gaussian
process with a basis expansion.

GPs are conceptually elegant, but as the timings above show, they get
slow as data sets get large. Basis-function approximations like the mesh/SPDE approach in
`sdmTMB` and `R-INLA` are messier conceptually, but they make large
data sets practical, along with extensions such as barriers and fields
that change through time. The mesh is one of several ways to
approximate a GP with basis functions. Another is the **Hilbert space
Gaussian process** (HSGP), which `brms` uses when you ask for
it.^[An HSGP (Solin and Särkkä 2020, *Stat. Comput.* 30: 419-446;
Riutort-Mayol et al. 2023, *Stat. Comput.* 33: 17) writes the field as
a sum of sine-shaped basis functions on a box around the data, with
weights whose prior variances come from the kernel. The GP becomes a
linear model with a prior on its weights, much like a penalized spline.
In `brms`, `gp(x_km, y_km, k = 20)` uses it, with `k` setting the
number of basis functions; without `k`, `gp()` fits the exact GP. It works best
with one to three coordinates. `mgcv`'s `bs = "gp"` smooth is also a
reduced-rank approximation. Other fast methods, such as
nearest-neighbor GPs (the `spNNGP` package), make the precision matrix
sparse without a basis expansion.]

Getting back to the mesh/SPDE approach: the main user decision is the mesh itself. 
Too coarse, and the tents can't
follow the field; finer than needed, and the fit slows for nothing.

```{r widget-mesh, echo=FALSE}
widget("spatial_mesh.html")
```

> **Question:** With the field's range at 10 km, start with a mesh edge
> length of 15 km and shorten it. At what edge length does the mesh
> version stop improving in any way you'd care about? Now set the range
> to 4 km and repeat. What rule relates the two?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* little is gained below an edge of about a third of the range
(range 10 km: edge 3; range 4 km: edge 1.5 gives correlation 0.99). The
edge has to be a fraction of the range, so the mesh depends on the
field, not on the number of plots.
```

## 5. One model, two packages {#packages}

Both packages below fit the model of [section 3](#gp-space).^[Other
packages fit it too. `nlme::gls()` takes a spatial correlation structure
the way it took AR(1) on the [Week 12 page](Week12_MixedModels.html#ar1);
see the [bonus section](#bonus-gls) below. It handles Normal responses
only and slows down past a few hundred locations. `spmodel::splm()` has
`lm()`-style syntax, `splm(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km, data = cg,
spcov_type = "exponential", xcoord = x_km, ycoord = y_km)`, with built-in
prediction and approximations for large data sets; with
`estmethod = "ml"` (its default is REML) it matches the by-hand fit's
log-likelihood. All of these are for point data, measured at locations.
Areal data, summarized over polygons such as counties or watersheds,
usually get conditional or simultaneous autoregressive (CAR or SAR)
models, in which neighbors are defined by shared borders rather than
distance: `spdep` and `spatialreg`, `spmodel::spautor()`, or a `car()`
term in `brms`.] They differ in how they represent the field and how
they estimate.

**`glmmTMB`** builds the full covariance matrix, as we did. The
coordinates go into a `numFactor`, and the field is an `exp()` term
grouped by a factor with one level (all plots belong to the same
landscape):

```{r glmmtmb-fit}
library(glmmTMB)
cg$pos <- numFactor(cg$x_km, cg$y_km)
cg$all <- factor(1)
time_glmmtmb <- system.time(
  fit_glmmtmb <- glmmTMB(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km + exp(pos + 0 | all), data = cg)
)[["elapsed"]]
c(logLik(fit_glmmtmb), by_hand = -fit_hand$value)
```

Same model, same likelihood, same answer as `optim()`.^[Swap `exp()`
for `mat()` to fit a Matérn with the smoothness estimated, or `gau()`
for the squared exponential. Like our `optim()` fit, `glmmTMB` builds
the dense matrix, so it slows down past a thousand or so locations.]

**`sdmTMB`** uses the mesh. The model call is a `glmmTMB`-style formula
plus the mesh:

```{r sdmtmb-fit}
time_sdmtmb <- system.time(
  fit_sdmtmb <- sdmTMB(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km, data = cg, mesh = mesh, spatial = "on")
)[["elapsed"]]
fit_sdmtmb
```

It maximizes the likelihood, integrating over the vertex values with
the [Laplace approximation](Week12_MixedModels.html#glmm-by-hand)
(exact here, since everything is Normal). In its output, `Spatial SD`
is $\sigma_s$, `Dispersion parameter` is $\sigma_e$, and `Matérn range`
is the range.

```{r compare-table, echo=FALSE}
td <- tidy(fit_sdmtmb)
tr <- tidy(fit_sdmtmb, "ran_pars")
tr <- setNames(tr$estimate, tr$term)
th <- exp(getME(fit_glmmtmb, "theta"))
se_g <- summary(fit_glmmtmb)$coefficients$cond[, 2]
cmp <- rbind(
  "Truth" = c(0.5, NA, -2, NA, 0.7, 12, 0.3, NA),
  "`lm()`, no spatial term" = c(coef(fit_lm)[2], lm_tab[2, 2], coef(fit_lm)[3], lm_tab[3, 2], NA, NA,
                                 sigma(fit_lm), NA),
  "`optim()`, exponential" = c(fit_hand$par[2], se_hand[2], fit_hand$par[3], se_hand[3], est_hand["sigma_s"],
                                2 * est_hand["ell"], est_hand["sigma_e"], NA),
  "`glmmTMB`, exponential" = c(fixef(fit_glmmtmb)$cond[2], se_g[2], fixef(fit_glmmtmb)$cond[3], se_g[3], th[1],
                                2 * th[2], sigma(fit_glmmtmb), time_glmmtmb),
  "`sdmTMB`, mesh (Matérn)" = c(td$estimate[2], td$std.error[2], td$estimate[3], td$std.error[3], tr["sigma_O"],
                                 tr["range"], tr["phi"], time_sdmtmb))
cmp_cols <- c("Fire", "SE", "Elevation", "SE", "$\\sigma_s$", "Range (km)", "$\\sigma_e$", "Seconds")
show_cmp <- function(m) {
  out <- data.frame(formatC(m[, 1:5], format = "f", digits = 2), formatC(m[, 6], format = "f", digits = 1),
                    formatC(m[, 7], format = "f", digits = 2), formatC(m[, 8], format = "f", digits = 1),
                    check.names = FALSE)
  out[] <- lapply(out, function(col) ifelse(grepl("NA", col), "", col))
  knitr::kable(out, col.names = cmp_cols, align = "r")
}
show_cmp(cmp)
```

For the exponential fits, the range is $2\hat\ell$.

The three spatial fits agree on the fire effect to within a fraction of
a standard error, although `sdmTMB` uses a different correlation
function from the one the data were simulated with. The mesh fit does
put more of the variance in $\sigma_e$ (0.42 against 0.27). Its
Matérn field is smoother than an exponential one,^[It has smoothness
$\nu = 1$, against $1/2$ for the exponential; see the
[Matérn bonus](#bonus-matern).] and a mesh
can't represent variation finer than its triangles, so the roughest
part of the field gets counted as plot-level noise.

Each package has its own names for the same parameters:

| | $\sigma_s$ | reach of correlation | $\sigma_e$ |
|:------------|:--------------------|:--------------------|:--------------------|
| `glmmTMB` `exp()` | `Std.Dev.` of the `all` group in `VarCorr()` | $\ell$: `exp(getME(fit, "theta"))[2]` | `sigma(fit)` |
| `sdmTMB` | `Spatial SD` (`sigma_O`) | `Matérn range` (about $2\ell$) | `Dispersion parameter` (`phi`) |

Which to use?

- **`glmmTMB`** when you already have a `glmmTMB` model and up to a
  thousand or so locations: the spatial term is one more piece of the
  formula, next to random effects, zero inflation, and the rest.
- **`sdmTMB`** for larger data sets and for maps: fast, a short
  syntax, built-in prediction, simulation, and cross-validation, and
  fields that change over time (`spatiotemporal = "ar1"`), and barriers
  the field can't cross, such as a coastline.^[Barrier meshes come from
  the companion package `sdmTMBextra` (`add_barrier_mesh()`, which takes
  the mesh and an `sf` polygon of the barrier; load `sdmTMBextra` after
  `sdmTMB`). They use the barrier model of Bakka et al. (2019,
  *Spatial Statistics*), also available in `R-INLA`: triangles inside the
  barrier get a much shorter range, so correlation has to travel around
  it rather than across.] It was written for species distribution models
  from survey data.
- **`R-INLA`**, through `inlabru`, when you want posteriors and priors,
  or model parts the others lack (several likelihoods sharing a field,
  many kinds of random effect, point patterns). It has the steepest
  learning curve of the three; the [bonus section](#bonus-inla) fits
  this model with it.

## 6. The GAM alternative: a smooth of the coordinates {#gam-space}

A penalized spline and a Gaussian process are two ways of building a
smooth surface ([section 4](#mesh)), so the spatial surface can also be
a [GAM smooth](Week13_HierarchicalModelsAndGAMs.html#gam) of the two
coordinates:

```{r gam-fit}
library(mgcv)
fit_gam <- gam(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km + s(x_km, y_km, k = 100), data = cg, method = "REML")
summary(fit_gam)$p.table
summary(fit_gam)$s.table
```

`s(x_km, y_km)` is a thin plate spline, the two-dimensional relative of
last week's curve: basis functions over the map, a penalty on the
surface's curvature, and REML to choose the penalty. `mgcv` can also
build the smooth from a Gaussian process kernel:

```{r gam-gp-fit}
fit_gam_gp <- gam(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km + s(x_km, y_km, bs = "gp", m = 2, k = 100),
                  data = cg, method = "REML")       # m = 2: exponential correlation
summary(fit_gam_gp)$p.table
```

```{r compare-table-gam, echo=FALSE}
pg <- summary(fit_gam)$p.table
pgg <- summary(fit_gam_gp)$p.table
cmp2 <- rbind(cmp[c(1, 3, 5), ],
              "`gam()`, thin plate spline" = c(pg[2, 1:2], pg[3, 1:2], NA, NA, sqrt(fit_gam$sig2), NA),
              "`gam()`, `bs = \"gp\"`" = c(pgg[2, 1:2], pgg[3, 1:2], NA, NA, sqrt(fit_gam_gp$sig2), NA))
out2 <- data.frame(formatC(cmp2[, c(1:4, 7)], format = "f", digits = 2), check.names = FALSE)
out2[] <- lapply(out2, function(col) ifelse(grepl("NA", col), "", col))
knitr::kable(out2,
             col.names = c("Fire", "SE", "Elevation", "SE", "$\\sigma_e$"), align = "r")
```

```{r gam-numbers, echo=FALSE}
elev_r2 <- summary(lm(elev_km ~ x_km + y_km, data = cg))$r.squared
pred_sd <- predict(fit_sdmtmb, newdata = grid)
gam_terms <- predict(fit_gam, newdata = grid, type = "terms")
gam_surface <- gam_terms[, "s(x_km,y_km)"]
```

The GAMs give nearly the same fire effect as the random field models.
Elevation is another matter: its standard error under the thin plate
spline is `r f1(pg[3, 2])`, against `r f2(se_hand[3])` for the
exponential field (and `r f1(pgg[3, 2])` with `bs = "gp"`). Both `mgcv`
smooths leave planes unpenalized (any flat tilt of the surface costs
nothing), and in this landscape
elevation is close to a tilted plane: easting and northing alone
explain `r round(100 * elev_r2)`% of its variation. The smooth can
stand in for elevation at no cost, so the data can't say how much of
the east-west gradient belongs to which. The random field has mean zero
and a finite range, which leaves broad gradients mostly to the
covariates.^[This is the spatial confounding from
[section 3](#gp-space). It affects every model
on this page to some degree (compare the elevation SEs from `lm()` and
the field models), and no choice of package removes it. Adding a
penalty on the planes (`select = TRUE` in `gam()`) helps only a little
here.]

```{r surface-maps, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=3}
zl_f <- c(-1.6, 1.6)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5))
map_image(grid$field_true, zl_f, pal_div, "True field")
map_fires(lty = 2)
map_image(pred_sd$omega_s, zl_f, pal_div, "sdmTMB random field")
points(cg$x_km, cg$y_km, pch = ".", cex = 2)
map_image(gam_surface - mean(gam_surface), zl_f, pal_div, "GAM thin plate smooth")
points(cg$x_km, cg$y_km, pch = ".", cex = 2)
```

The left map is the field the data were simulated from (blue below
zero, red above). The fitted field's correlation with it across the
grid is `r f2(cor(pred_sd$omega_s, grid$field_true))`; the GAM smooth's
is `r f2(cor(gam_surface, grid$field_true))`, lower partly because the
smooth has also taken on some of the elevation gradient.

**Which approach, when?** The two are close relatives, and for many
data sets either will do.^[Miller, Glennie, and Seaton (2020, *J.
Agric. Biol. Environ. Stat.* 25: 1-16) show that the mesh-based random
field can itself be fit as an `mgcv` smooth with a custom penalty.]
Some things do favor one or the other:

| Situation | Leans toward | Why |
|:-------------------------------|:---------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Space is a nuisance: you want valid SEs for covariates and a rough map of what's left | GAM smooth | one extra term in `gam()`; nothing to build or tune beyond `k` |
| You want the scale of dependence itself: how far does similarity reach, how much variance is spatial | random field | $\ell$ and $\sigma_s$ are parameters with standard errors; a smooth has only an edf (in `bs = "gp"` the range is fixed in advance, not estimated) |
| Prediction away from the data, with honest uncertainty | random field | the field returns to zero and its SE to $\sigma_s$ beyond the range; a thin plate spline keeps extending its last tilt |
| A field that changes through time (annual surveys, tracking a range shift) | random field | `sdmTMB` and `R-INLA` have spatiotemporal fields (independent, random walk, AR(1)) built in |

The [bonus section](#bonus-which) has more cases (other smooths in the
model, patchy fields, a covariate that is smooth in space, very large
data sets, barriers, Bayesian fits).

Whichever you choose, check the residuals for leftover spatial pattern
([below](#demo-check)).

## Discussion {#spatial-discussion}

**Q1.** The ordinary regression puts the fire effect at
`r f2(coef(fit_lm)[2])` (SE `r f2(lm_tab["burned", 2])`); the spatial
models put it near `r f2(fit_hand$par[2])` (SE `r f2(se_hand[2])`). A
colleague objects: "Fire scars are spatial patches. Your random field
is a patchy surface. It has soaked up half of the fire effect." How
would you respond? What survey design would have made the two easier
to separate?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* the worry is legitimate in general (spatial confounding), but
here the truth is 0.5, so the field removed bias, not signal. What
identifies the fire effect is the contrast across fire boundaries
between plots close enough to share the field. A better design pairs
plots just inside and just outside each perimeter, and samples more
fires.
```

**Q2.** The elevation coefficient has a standard error of
`r f2(lm_tab["elev_km", 2])` in the ordinary regression,
`r f2(se_hand[3])` with an exponential random field, and
`r f1(pg[3, 2])` with a thin plate smooth. The estimates are
`r f2(coef(fit_lm)[3])`, `r f2(fit_hand$par[3])`, and `r f2(pg[3, 1])`.
Which would you report to the district, and what would you say about
it?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* report the random field's estimate with its wide interval
(about -2.6 to -0.3) and say the survey can't separate elevation from
other east-west gradients. The lm() SE is wrong for the same reason as
the fire SE; the GAM's SE says the smooth and elevation are
interchangeable. Truth is -2.
```

**Q3.** The random field stands in for whatever varies smoothly across
the landscape and isn't in the model. Look at the fitted field in the
maps above. If you could add one field season of measurements, what
would you measure and where, and what would you expect to happen to
$\hat\sigma_s$ if you guessed right?

## Bonus: more on choosing a smooth or a random field {#bonus-which}

More situations that favor one approach or the other, beyond those in
[section 6](#gam-space):

| Situation | Leans toward | Why |
|:-------------------------------|:---------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| The model already has other smooths (season, depth, a nonlinear covariate) | GAM smooth | everything in one `mgcv` formula; `te()` and `by =` for surfaces that change with a covariate |
| Fine-scale, patchy variation relative to plot spacing | random field | exponential and Matérn fields are rough; a smooth with moderate `k` captures broad trends and can leave short-range correlation in the residuals |
| A covariate of interest is itself smooth in space | random field, with care | a mean-zero field with finite range competes less for broad gradients; check how the coefficient moves either way |
| Tens of thousands of locations or more | either | `mgcv::bam()` or a mesh; not a dense covariance matrix |
| Coastlines, lakes, and other barriers | either, specialized | soap film smooths in `mgcv`; barrier models in `R-INLA` and `sdmTMB` |
| Bayesian inference with informative priors | random field in `R-INLA`, or either in `brms` | `brms` takes `s()` and `gp()` terms; MCMC with a Gaussian process is slow beyond a few hundred points |

## Bonus: the Matérn family {#bonus-matern}

The Matérn family has a second parameter besides the length-scale: the
smoothness $\nu$. The exponential is $\nu = 1/2$ (rough surfaces), and
as $\nu \to \infty$ the Matérn becomes last week's squared exponential
(very smooth surfaces). The mesh-based packages (`sdmTMB`, `R-INLA`)
use $\nu = 1$, which is in between. Smoothness is hard to estimate
from field data, so it is usually fixed. The Matérn correlation is

$$\rho(d) = \frac{2^{1-\nu}}{\Gamma(\nu)} (\kappa d)^\nu K_\nu(\kappa d)$$

with $K_\nu$ a modified Bessel function and $\kappa$ an inverse
length-scale; for $\nu = 1/2$ it reduces to $e^{-\kappa d}$. Packages
that use the Matérn report a **range**, $\sqrt{8\nu}/\kappa$, the
distance at which the correlation has fallen to about 0.13. For the
exponential that distance is $2\ell$.

## Bonus: a Bayesian fit with R-INLA {#bonus-inla}

`R-INLA` uses the same mesh and the same sparse precision matrix as
`sdmTMB`, and is Bayesian: it returns posterior distributions, computed by a
fast deterministic approximation in place of MCMC.^[INLA stands for
integrated nested Laplace approximation (Rue, Martino, and Chopin 2009,
*J. R. Stat. Soc. B* 71: 319-392). It applies to models whose
unobserved layer is Gaussian, which covers every model on this page.]
We call it through **`inlabru`**, a front end that writes the whole
model as one formula.^[`inlabru` builds the projection matrix `A` from
[section 4](#mesh) and the rest of INLA's input for you. Many older
tutorials call `inla()` directly, building `A` with
`inla.spde.make.A()` and bundling it with the data in an
`inla.stack()`; for this model the estimates are identical. `inlabru`
also fits predictors that are nonlinear in the parameters and
point-process models of species locations.] The plots go in as an `sf`
object, so the field term can find each plot's location (`geometry`),
and the field gets priors for its range and $\sigma_s$:

```{r inla-fit}
library(INLA)
library(inlabru)
library(sf)
cg_sf <- st_as_sf(cg, coords = c("x_km", "y_km"), remove = FALSE)   # plots as spatial points
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh$mesh,
                            prior.range = c(5, 0.5),     # P(range < 5 km) = 0.5
                            prior.sigma = c(1, 0.05))    # P(sigma_s > 1) = 0.05
fit_inla <- bru(log_biomass ~ Intercept(1) + burned + elev_km + field(geometry, model = spde),
                data = cg_sf, family = "gaussian")
round(fit_inla$summary.fixed[, c("mean", "sd", "0.025quant", "0.975quant")], 3)
round(fit_inla$summary.hyperpar[, c("mean", "0.025quant", "0.5quant", "0.975quant")], 3)
```

The priors are *penalized complexity* priors, which are stated as tail
probabilities: here, an even chance that the range is under 5 km, and a
5% chance that $\sigma_s$ is over 1.^[Fuglstad et al. (2019, *J. Am.
Stat. Assoc.* 114: 445-452). The prior shrinks the field toward a
simpler model (a long range and a small variance), so a field has to be
supported by the data to appear. `sdmTMB` accepts the same priors
through `sdmTMBpriors()` and `pc_matern()`, and `glmmTMB` has a
`priors` argument. Neither package samples a posterior, though. A prior
there adds its log density to the log-likelihood, and the fit maximizes
the sum, so the estimates are posterior modes (maximum a posteriori, or
MAP), and the standard errors still come from the curvature at the
peak. The prior acts as a penalty, the way the ridge penalty acts as a
[Normal prior](Week13_HierarchicalModelsAndGAMs.html#ridge-prior): it
keeps a parameter the data say little about, such as a long range or a
variance near zero, from running off to an extreme. For a full
posterior, both packages can pass the same model to Stan through the
`tmbstan` package (in `sdmTMB`, fit with `bayesian = TRUE` first).] In the output, `Stdev for field` is $\sigma_s$, `Range for field` is
the range, and `Precision for the Gaussian observations` is
$1/\sigma_e^2$.

```{r inla-numbers, echo=FALSE}
hy <- fit_inla$summary.hyperpar
```

The posterior mean fire effect is
`r f2(fit_inla$summary.fixed["burned", "mean"])` (posterior SD
`r f2(fit_inla$summary.fixed["burned", "sd"])`), against
`r f2(td$estimate[2])` (SE `r f2(td$std.error[2])`) from `sdmTMB`. The
posterior medians are `r f2(hy["Stdev for field", "0.5quant"])` for
$\sigma_s$, `r f1(hy["Range for field", "0.5quant"])` km for the range,
and `r f2(1 / sqrt(hy[1, "0.5quant"]))` for $\sigma_e$, close to
`sdmTMB`'s `r f2(tr["sigma_O"])`, `r f1(tr["range"])`, and
`r f2(tr["phi"])`.

## Bonus: a spatial term in brms {#bonus-brms}

For a fully Bayesian fit by MCMC, `brms` accepts both forms: an `mgcv`
smooth, `s(x_km, y_km, k = 100)`, fit as a random effect as in
[last week's bonus](Week13_HierarchicalModelsAndGAMs.html#smooth-brms),
or a Gaussian process, `gp(x_km, y_km)`. An exact `gp()` builds the
dense covariance matrix at every MCMC step, which is slow for 200 plots
and impractical for thousands; `gp(x_km, y_km, k = 20, c = 5/4)` uses a
basis-function approximation that scales much better. Neither is run
here.

## Bonus: the same model with `gls()` in nlme {#bonus-gls}

`gls()` from `nlme` fits the model of [section 3](#gp-space) with a
spatial correlation structure in place of the AR(1) structure on the
[Week 12 page](Week12_MixedModels.html#ar1). Like the by-hand fit and
`glmmTMB`, it builds the full covariance matrix.

```{r gls-fit}
library(nlme)
fit_gls <- gls(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km, data = cg, method = "ML",
               correlation = corExp(form = ~ x_km + y_km, nugget = TRUE))
round(summary(fit_gls)$tTable, 3)
c(logLik_gls = as.numeric(logLik(fit_gls)), logLik_by_hand = -fit_hand$value)
```

The coefficients and log-likelihood match the by-hand fit. `gls()`
reports the covariance parameters differently: its `range` is $\ell$,
its `nugget` is the nugget's share of the total variance,
$\sigma_e^2 / (\sigma_s^2 + \sigma_e^2)$, and its residual standard
error is the total SD, $\sqrt{\sigma_s^2 + \sigma_e^2}$. Converting
back:

```{r gls-params}
gls_cor <- coef(fit_gls$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)
total_sd <- sigma(fit_gls)
round(c(sigma_s = total_sd * sqrt(1 - gls_cor[["nugget"]]), ell = gls_cor[["range"]],
        sigma_e = total_sd * sqrt(gls_cor[["nugget"]])), 3)
intervals(fit_gls, which = "var-cov")
```

```{r gls-numbers, echo=FALSE}
gls_ci <- intervals(fit_gls, which = "var-cov")$corStruct
fit_gls_reml <- update(fit_gls, method = "REML")
```

The approximate 95% interval for the range runs from
`r f1(gls_ci["range", "lower"])` to `r f1(gls_ci["range", "upper"])` km
(the truth is 6): 200 plots say roughly how far the correlation
reaches, not much more.^[`method = "ML"` makes `gls()` match the
by-hand likelihood. Its default, REML, corrects the variance parameters
for the regression coefficients having been estimated (the same
correction `lmer()` makes); here it gives $\hat\ell$ =
`r f1(coef(fit_gls_reml$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)[["range"]])`
km and a fire effect of
`r f2(coef(fit_gls_reml)[["burned"]])`. Compare models with different
fixed effects by AIC only under ML. `corExp()` can be swapped for
`corGaus()`, `corSpher()`, and others; `corMatern()` is not in `nlme`
itself.] `gls()` is limited to Normal responses; for counts or
presence/absence, use `glmmTMB` or `sdmTMB`.

# A spatial analysis from start to finish {#demo}

This part takes the cheatgrass survey from the district's two questions
to an answer: candidate models, a mesh, checks on the fit, comparison
by AIC and by two kinds of cross-validation, and maps of predicted
biomass with their uncertainty. It uses `sdmTMB` throughout.

## 1. Problem and candidate models {#demo-problem}

```{r workflow-all, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow(c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES"))
```

The district's questions again: how much does a past fire raise
cheatgrass biomass, and where is biomass above its treatment threshold
of 60 g per square meter (log biomass above `r f2(log(60))`)?

Three candidate models:

- **M0, no spatial term.** Fire and elevation explain what there is to
  explain; the rest is plot-level noise.
- **M1, spatial.** Fire and elevation, plus a random field for
  unmeasured conditions shared by neighbors.
- **M2, spatial with an interaction.** As M1, with a fire effect that
  changes with elevation (cheatgrass does poorly at high, cold sites
  whether or not they burned).

Two practical points before fitting. Coordinates should be projected,
in units that make distances meaningful, and scaled so the range is a
moderate number: kilometers here, not meters and not degrees of
longitude and latitude.^[A degree of longitude is about 85 km at Reno's
latitude and a degree of latitude about 111 km, so distances computed
from raw degrees are wrong in a direction-dependent way. With
longitude/latitude data, project first: `sdmTMB::add_utm_columns()`
does it in one step, or use `sf::st_transform()`.] And center
covariates so the intercept means something (elevation is in km above
1800 m).

## 2. The mesh {#demo-mesh}

`make_mesh()` needs one decision, the resolution. `cutoff` is the
shortest edge allowed, in the units of the coordinates. A common
starting point is an edge length of a third to a fifth of the range you
expect, and the residual [variogram](#variogram) suggested the range is
around 10 km. Then check that the answers don't depend on the choice:

```{r mesh-sensitivity, cache=TRUE}
mesh_check <- t(sapply(c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8), function(co) {
  m <- make_mesh(cg, c("x_km", "y_km"), cutoff = co)
  f <- sdmTMB(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km, data = cg, mesh = m, spatial = "on")
  rp <- tidy(f, "ran_pars")
  c(cutoff = co, vertices = m$mesh$n, fire = tidy(f)$estimate[2], fire_se = tidy(f)$std.error[2],
    range = rp$estimate[rp$term == "range"], sigma_s = rp$estimate[rp$term == "sigma_O"],
    logLik = as.numeric(logLik(f)))
}))
round(mesh_check, 2)
```

With cutoffs of 1 to 3 km the fire effect and its standard error hardly
move. The range and $\sigma_s$ move more, which says how loosely the
data determine them. At 5 km the log-likelihood drops, and at 8 km the
fit falls apart (look at the range). We keep the 2-km mesh from
[above](#mesh).

> **Question:** The 1-km mesh has almost twice the vertices of the 2-km
> mesh. What did the extra vertices buy? When would you need them?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* nothing here (same estimates, log-likelihood about -172.4 vs.
-172.9). Extra vertices are needed when the range is short relative to
2 km, or plots are dense enough to show finer structure.
```

## 3. Fit and check {#demo-check}

```{r demo-fits}
m0 <- sdmTMB(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km, data = cg, spatial = "off")
m1 <- sdmTMB(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km, data = cg, mesh = mesh, spatial = "on")
m2 <- sdmTMB(log_biomass ~ burned * elev_km, data = cg, mesh = mesh, spatial = "on")
```

```{r demo-sanity, message=TRUE}
sanity(m1)
```

`sanity()` runs the checks you would otherwise do by hand after
`optim()`: did the optimizer converge, is the Hessian usable, are any
standard errors or variance parameters suspicious.

Then the residuals, the goodness-of-fit part of COMPARE. If the field
has done its job, what's left should look like independent noise. The
`DHARMa` package checks this by simulation: it simulates many new data
sets from the fitted model and asks where each observation falls among
its own simulated values. If the model is right, those positions
(scaled residuals between 0 and 1) are uniform, whatever the response
distribution.^[See the `DHARMa` vignette (Hartig, on CRAN). A scaled residual of
0.5 means the observation sits in the middle of its simulations; 0 or
1 means it is more extreme than all of them. The same calls work for
counts, presence/absence, and any other family `sdmTMB` fits.]
`sdmTMB` supplies the simulations, and `dharma_residuals()` hands them
to `DHARMa`:

```{r demo-dharma, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5}
library(DHARMa)
set.seed(746)
dh_m1 <- dharma_residuals(simulate(m1, nsim = 250, type = "mle-mvn"), m1, return_DHARMa = TRUE, plot = FALSE)
plot(dh_m1)
```

The left panel is a QQ plot of the scaled residuals against a uniform
distribution, with three tests: uniformity (KS), dispersion, and
outliers. The right panel plots the residuals against the predictions;
the quantile lines should run flat at 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75.

```{r demo-dharma-tests, echo=FALSE}
dh_unif <- testUniformity(dh_m1, plot = FALSE)
dh_disp <- testDispersion(dh_m1, plot = FALSE)
```

The uniformity test passes (p = `r f2(dh_unif$p.value)`). The
dispersion test and the right panel both flag the same thing: the
residuals bunch toward 0.5 (dispersion ratio `r f2(dh_disp$statistic)`,
and the outer quantile lines sit inside 0.25 and 0.75). That is an
artifact, not a problem with the model.^[The simulations keep the fitted field, which sits
partly on top of the observations, so the observed values are closer
to the predictions than fresh noise would be. Refitting M1 to six data
sets simulated from the true model gave dispersion ratios of about 0.45
to 0.7, every one flagged, and the quantile test in the right panel
flagged four of the six. The same happens with a Poisson field model.
To check for overdispersion in a count model, compare Poisson and
negative binomial (`nbinom2()`) fits by AIC instead.] Check what a test
assumes before acting on it.

For spatial data the key test is whether neighbors' residuals still
resemble each other. `testSpatialAutocorrelation()` computes Moran's
$I$ on the residuals; M0, without a field, is the contrast:

```{r demo-moran}
dh_m0 <- dharma_residuals(simulate(m0, nsim = 250, type = "mle-mvn"), m0, return_DHARMa = TRUE, plot = FALSE)
sa_m0 <- testSpatialAutocorrelation(dh_m0, x = cg$x_km, y = cg$y_km, plot = FALSE)
sa_m1 <- testSpatialAutocorrelation(dh_m1, x = cg$x_km, y = cg$y_km, plot = FALSE)
round(rbind(M0 = c(sa_m0$statistic["observed"], p = sa_m0$p.value),
            M1 = c(sa_m1$statistic["observed"], p = sa_m1$p.value)), 3)
```

A residual variogram shows the same thing, and shows how far the
pattern reaches:

```{r demo-residuals}
cg$resid_m1 <- residuals(m1, type = "mle-mvn")
cg_sp$resid_m1 <- cg$resid_m1
cg_sp$resid_m0 <- as.numeric(scale(cg$resid_lm))
vg_m0 <- variogram(resid_m0 ~ 1, cg_sp, cutoff = 20, width = 2)
vg_m1 <- variogram(resid_m1 ~ 1, cg_sp, cutoff = 20, width = 2)
```

```{r demo-residual-plots, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(vg_m0$dist, vg_m0$gamma, pch = 1, ylim = c(0, 1.5), xlim = c(0, 20), xlab = "Distance between plots (km)",
     ylab = "Semivariance of standardized residuals")
points(vg_m1$dist, vg_m1$gamma, pch = 16, col = "#2a78d6")
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
legend("bottomright", c("M0 (no spatial term)", "M1 (spatial)"), pch = c(1, 16), col = c("black", "#2a78d6"),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

M0's residuals are strongly autocorrelated (Moran's $I$ p
`r if (sa_m0$p.value < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste("=", f2(sa_m0$p.value))`),
and its variogram rises with distance. M1's are not (p =
`r f2(sa_m1$p.value)`), and its variogram is flat near 1 at every
distance: no spatial pattern is left.^[These variogram residuals come
from `residuals(m1, type = "mle-mvn")`, randomized quantile residuals
on the Normal scale with the random field drawn from its estimated
distribution, the choice `sdmTMB` recommends. They are the Normal-scale
version of `DHARMa`'s scaled residuals.]

## 4. Compare {#demo-compare}

```{r workflow-compare, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow("COMPARE")
```

```{r demo-aic}
aic <- AIC(m0, m1, m2)
aic$dAIC <- aic$AIC - min(aic$AIC)
aic
tidy(m2)
```

M1 is best. The interaction costs a parameter and buys nothing, so M2
is an example of an
[uninformative parameter](Week10_ModelComparison.html#frequentist):
within 2 AIC units of the best model only because it contains it. M0
is far behind.

AIC asks how well each model would predict new data like the data in
hand. The district's second question is about prediction at places
without plots, so it is worth asking directly with
[cross-validation](Week10_ModelComparison.html#cross-validation), and
here spatial data set a trap. If plots are held out at random, each
held-out plot has neighbors still in the training set, and the random
field can predict it from them. That is a fair test of filling gaps
inside the survey, and a poor test of predicting a new area. For the
second, hold out whole blocks:

```{r demo-cv, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(746)
fold_random <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(cg)))                           # 10 random folds
fold_block <- as.integer(factor(paste(floor(cg$x_km / 10), floor(cg$y_km / 10))))  # 10-km blocks
cv_rmse <- function(formula, spatial, folds) {
  cv <- sdmTMB_cv(formula, data = cg, mesh = mesh, spatial = spatial, fold_ids = folds)
  sqrt(mean((cv$data$cv_predicted - cv$data$log_biomass)^2))
}
cv_tab <- rbind(
  random_folds = c(M0 = cv_rmse(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km, "off", fold_random),
                   M1 = cv_rmse(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km, "on", fold_random)),
  block_folds = c(M0 = cv_rmse(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km, "off", fold_block),
                  M1 = cv_rmse(log_biomass ~ burned + elev_km, "on", fold_block)))
round(cv_tab, 3)                  # root mean squared prediction error, log biomass
```

```{r demo-blocks-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4.6}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
map_base("Block folds: each 10-km square is held out in turn")
abline(v = seq(10, 30, 10), h = c(10, 20), col = "grey60", lty = 2)
points(cg$x_km, cg$y_km, pch = 21, bg = hcl.colors(12, "Set 3")[fold_block], cex = 1.1)
```

With random folds the spatial model's prediction error is
`r round(100 * (1 - cv_tab[1, 2] / cv_tab[1, 1]))`% lower than M0's.
With whole 10-km blocks held out, the two models predict about equally
well (`r f2(cv_tab[2, 1])` and `r f2(cv_tab[2, 2])`): a block's
center is farther from the remaining plots than the field's
correlation reaches, so the field has little to offer there and
prediction falls back on fire and elevation.^[Roberts et al. (2017,
*Ecography* 40: 913-929) review blocking strategies for spatial,
temporal, and grouped data.]

> **Question:** The district wants a map of the surveyed area,
> including the roadless block. Which of the two cross-validation
> results describes how well that map will do, and where on the map
> does each one apply?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* random folds describe cells with plots within a few km (most
of the map); block folds describe the middle of the roadless block and
anywhere beyond the survey edge.
```

## 5. Predict {#demo-predict}

Prediction at a new location uses everything the model knows: the
regression part, from that location's fire history and elevation, plus
the field's value there, inferred from nearby plots. For the model of
[section 3](#gp-space) this is the conditional mean of a multivariate
Normal, the same formula that drew last week's
[Gaussian process curve](Week13_HierarchicalModelsAndGAMs.html#gp)
between cultures. Geostatistics calls it **kriging**.

The prediction grid has a row for each half-kilometer cell, with the
same covariates as the plots:

```{r demo-predict}
pred <- predict(m1, newdata = grid)
head(pred[, c("x_km", "y_km", "est", "est_non_rf", "omega_s")], 3)
set.seed(746)
sims <- predict(m1, newdata = grid, nsim = 500)      # 500 draws of the predicted surface
pred$se <- apply(sims, 1, sd)
pred$p_exceed <- rowMeans(sims > log(60))            # P(expected log biomass is above the threshold)
```

`est` is the prediction, `est_non_rf` its regression part, and
`omega_s` the field. Calling `predict()` with `nsim` returns draws
from the joint uncertainty in the coefficients and the field, one
column per draw, which turns any question about the map into a
calculation on the columns.^[The draws are of the expected log biomass
in each cell. They leave out the plot-level noise $\sigma_e$, so they
answer "what is typical here?" and not "what would one clipped quadrat
weigh?" To report biomass on its original scale, note that
$e^{\text{est}}$ is the median; the mean is
$e^{\text{est} + \sigma^2/2}$, with $\sigma^2$ the variance left
around the prediction.]

```{r demo-maps, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=7.4}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5))
map_image(pred$est_non_rf, zl_y, pal_seq, "Regression part: fire and elevation")
map_key(zl_y, pal_seq, "log biomass")
map_image(pred$est, zl_y, pal_seq, "Prediction: regression + field")
points(cg$x_km, cg$y_km, pch = ".", cex = 2)
map_image(pred$se, c(0.1, 0.5), hcl.colors(64, "Purples", rev = TRUE), "Standard error of the prediction")
points(cg$x_km, cg$y_km, pch = ".", cex = 2)
rect(13, 1, 22, 10, border = "grey30", lty = 3)
map_key(c(0.1, 0.5), hcl.colors(64, "Purples", rev = TRUE), "SE", digits = 2)
map_image(pred$p_exceed, c(0, 1), hcl.colors(64, "Reds", rev = TRUE), "P(biomass above 60 g per square meter)")
contour(ux, uy, matrix(pred$p_exceed, length(ux)), levels = 0.5, drawlabels = FALSE, add = TRUE, lwd = 1.5)
map_key(c(0, 1), hcl.colors(64, "Reds", rev = TRUE), "probability", digits = 2)
```

```{r demo-truth, echo=FALSE}
pred0 <- predict(m0, newdata = grid)
rmse_m0 <- sqrt(mean((pred0$est - grid$log_biomass_true)^2))
rmse_m1 <- sqrt(mean((pred$est - grid$log_biomass_true)^2))
roadless <- grid$x_km > 13 & grid$x_km < 22 & grid$y_km > 1 & grid$y_km < 10
above <- grid$log_biomass_true > log(60)
flag <- pred$p_exceed > 0.5
```

The regression part alone (top left) is a map of fire perimeters
shaded by elevation. The field adds the patches the covariates miss.
The standard error is lowest next to plots and highest in the roadless
block and at the corners (mean `r f2(mean(pred$se[roadless]))` in the
block, `r f2(mean(pred$se[!roadless]))` elsewhere). The last map is
the one that answers the district's question: the probability that
each cell is above the threshold, with a contour at 0.5.

Since the data are simulated, the true surface is known. Across the
grid, M1's predictions miss the true log biomass by
`r f2(rmse_m1)` (root mean squared error), against `r f2(rmse_m0)` for
M0. Of the cells flagged with probability above 0.5,
`r round(100 * mean(above[flag]))`% are truly above the threshold, and
the flagged cells include `r round(100 * mean(flag[above]))`% of all
cells that are.

> **Question:** The district can treat only a quarter of the area the
> map flags. Would you send crews to the cells with the highest
> predicted biomass, or the highest probability of exceeding the
> threshold? Where do the two rankings disagree?

```{asis, echo=FALSE}
*Land:* probability, if the goal is not to waste treatment. The
rankings disagree where the SE is high: a cell far from plots can have
a high prediction and a modest probability. That is a case for sampling
there first.
```

## 6. What we tell the district {#demo-answer}

```{r demo-answer, echo=FALSE}
b1 <- tidy(m1, conf.int = TRUE)
rp1 <- tidy(m1, "ran_pars", conf.int = TRUE)
```

- **Fire.** Burned plots carry about `r f1(exp(b1$estimate[2]))` times
  the cheatgrass biomass of comparable unburned plots (95% interval
  `r f1(exp(b1$conf.low[2]))` to `r f1(exp(b1$conf.high[2]))`). A
  regression that ignored the spatial pattern put this at
  `r f1(exp(coef(fit_lm)[2]))` times, with a standard error less than
  half of what it should have been.
- **Elevation.** Biomass falls with elevation, but this survey can't
  say how steeply (95% interval for the slope
  `r f1(b1$conf.low[3])` to `r f1(b1$conf.high[3])` per km).
- **Unmeasured conditions.** Something not in the model varies over
  distances of about `r round(rp1$estimate[rp1$term == "range"])` km
  and moves log biomass about as much as fire does ($\hat\sigma_s =$
  `r f2(rp1$estimate[rp1$term == "sigma_O"])`). The
  field map shows where; that is where to look for the next covariate.
- **The map.** Predictions are good near plots and no better than the
  covariates far from them. The roadless block needs plots before
  anyone should act on its predictions.

The spatial model is corroborated against two rivals, one without a
field and one with an interaction. It hasn't been tested against a
model with the missing covariate in it, because nobody has measured
that covariate yet.

## Bonus: counts and other responses {#demo-counts}

A random field goes into a GLM the way a random intercept does, on the
scale of the linear predictor. The survey also counted cheatgrass
seedlings in a small frame at each plot:

$$\text{seedlings}_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_i), \qquad
\log \mu_i = \mathbf{x}_i^T\boldsymbol\beta + s_i$$

```{r demo-counts}
fit_pois_glm <- glm(seedlings ~ burned + elev_km, data = cg, family = poisson)
fit_pois_sp <- sdmTMB(seedlings ~ burned + elev_km, data = cg, mesh = mesh, spatial = "on", family = poisson())
round(rbind(glm = summary(fit_pois_glm)$coefficients[2, 1:2],
            spatial = unlist(tidy(fit_pois_sp)[2, c("estimate", "std.error")])), 3)     # fire effect
```

The same thing happens as with log biomass: the fire coefficient moves
toward the truth (0.5) and its standard error more than doubles. The
likelihood can no longer be written as one multivariate Normal,
because the field has to be
[integrated out numerically](Week12_MixedModels.html#glmm-by-hand);
the packages do it with the Laplace approximation. Only the `family`
argument changes: `nbinom2()` for overdispersed counts, `binomial()`
for presence/absence, `tweedie()` or a delta model for biomass with
zeros. `glmmTMB` and `R-INLA` take the same step in their own syntax.

## A take-home exercise {#wod}

The WOD (workout of the day, a short exercise) that goes with this
page is
[*Neighbors*](wod/WOD_Week14_Lecture1_Neighbors.pdf). It uses a
different data set, snow measurements at 60 stations, and asks for the
piece this page leaves out: predicting at a new location by hand.
